title: Ῥόδον καὶ ἀμάραντον
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 323. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ῥόδῳ παραφυὲν ἀμάραντον ἔφη· « Οἷον ἄνθος εὐπρεπὲς εἶ, καὶ ποθητὸν καὶ θεοῖς καὶ ἀνθρώποις· μακαρίζω σε τοῦ κάλλους καὶ τῆς εὐωδίας. »
sentences.tr: Rhodōi paraphyen amaranton ephē· « Hoion anthos euprepes ei, kai pothēton kai theois kai anthrōpois· makarizō se tou kallous kai tēs euōdias. »
sentences.l: An amaranth grown up beside a rose said: « What a comely flower you are, and longed for both by gods and by men; I count you blessed for your beauty and your fragrance. »
sentences.n: ἀμάραντον is 'the unfading', from ἀ- and μαραίνω, 'to wither' — the name carries the whole fable. Both flowers are neuter nouns, ἀμάραντον here and ῥόδον below, so the adjectives on either side of the dialogue are neuter: εὐπρεπές and ποθητόν of the rose here, νέον of the amaranth at the end. παραφυέν is an aorist passive participle used intransitively, 'having grown up beside'. μακαρίζω takes a genitive of the ground on which one is called happy.

sentences.t: Τὸ δὲ εἶπεν· « Ἐγὼ μέν, ὦ ἀμάραντον, πρὸς ὀλίγον καιρὸν ζῶ, καί, κἂν μηδεὶς ἐκκόψῃ με, τήκομαι· σὺ δὲ ἀνθεῖς καὶ ζῇς ἀεὶ οὕτω νέον. »
sentences.tr: To de eipen· « Egō men, ō amaranton, pros oligon kairon zō, kai, kan mēdeis ekkopsēi me, tēkomai· sy de antheis kai zēis aei houtō neon. »
sentences.l: And it said: « I, O amaranth, live for a short season, and, even if no one cuts me down, I waste away; but you bloom and live for ever, young like this. »
sentences.i: And the rose answered: « Amaranth, I live only a little while, and even if nobody cuts me down I waste away of myself; but you flower and go on living, always as young as this. »
sentences.n: Τὸ δέ is the rose speaking — ῥόδον is neuter, so the article alone marks the change of speaker, as regularly in these dialogues. κἄν is καὶ ἐάν run together by crasis and takes the subjunctive ἐκκόψῃ, 'even if'. τήκομαι is to melt, to run away like snow: the rose is not killed, it simply goes. νέον is neuter, agreeing with the amaranth addressed.

sentences.t: Ὅτι κρεῖσσον ὀλιγαρκούμενόν τινα διαμένειν ἢ πρὸς ὀλίγον τρυφήσαντα μεταβολῆς δυστυχοῦς τυχεῖν ἢ καὶ ἀποθανεῖν.
sentences.tr: Hoti kreisson oligarkoumenon tina diamenein ē pros oligon tryphēsanta metabolēs dystychous tychein ē kai apothanein.
sentences.l: That it is better for one, content with little, to abide on than, having lived softly for a short time, to meet with an unhappy change or even to die.
sentences.i: The story shows that it is better to be content with little and last than to live delicately for a short while and then meet an unhappy turn of fortune, or even death.
sentences.n: A moral in the bare Ὅτι form: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek, which begins simply 'That…', and is supplied in the idiomatic line. κρεῖσσον, 'better', is followed by accusative and infinitive (τινα … διαμένειν), with the two participles ὀλιγαρκούμενον and τρυφήσαντα agreeing with τινα. τυγχάνω takes the genitive of what one meets with. καί before ἀποθανεῖν is 'even'.
